cards.text: Job has lost his children, his wealth and his health, and his friends keep telling him he must have done wrong to deserve it (Job 1:13-2:8; 22:5). Job keeps saying he's innocent (Job 10:7). Now he picks it right back up with his friends, and baker, this man is NOT done talking.
He opens with an oath, "As surely as God lives…" and in the same breath he says God has deprived him of justice and the Almighty has embittered his soul.

cards.question: Job makes a promise that lasts as long as there's breath in him. What does he promise his lips won't do?
Job tells his friends he's finally ready to admit they've been right.

cards.text: Job says he'll maintain his integrity until he dies. He'll cling to his righteousness and never let go, like someone holding the last cookie in the box while the whole family reaches for it.

cards.question: As long as Job lives, he says one thing won't accuse him. What is it?

cards.text: Then Job says, "May my enemy be like the wicked and my opponent like the unjust." Baker, that is NOT a get-well card.
And he asks what hope the godless man has when he is cut off, when God takes away his life.

cards.question: Job keeps asking about the godless man. When distress comes on him, what does Job wonder?
Job also asks whether the godless man will delight in the Almighty and call on God at all times.

cards.text: Now Job switches into teacher mode. He says, "I will instruct you in the power of God…"

cards.question: Job tells his friends, "Surely all of you have seen it for yourselves." So why do they keep up all this ___ talk?

cards.text: Now Job lays out the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage the ruthless receive from the Almighty.

cards.question: Job says that though the wicked man's sons are many, they will live long and peaceful lives.
Job keeps going: the wicked man's sons are destined for the sword, his offspring will never have enough food, and his survivors are buried by the plague. How do their widows respond?

cards.text: Next, his stuff. Job says that though the wicked man heaps up silver like dust and piles up a wardrobe like clay, there's a catch. Baker, I spent YEARS under the dust in the back of a junk drawer, so trust me, that's a LOT of silver.

cards.question: Job says the righteous end up wearing what the wicked man laid up.

cards.text: And his silver gets divided up by the innocent. As for the house he built, Job says it's like a moth's cocoon.

cards.question: Job compares the wicked man's house to a moth's cocoon. What other picture does he use for that house?

answers.text: A hut set up by a watchman
A tent pitched by a shepherd
A shelter made by a prophet

cards.question: The wicked man lies down ___, but when he opens his eyes, all is gone.

cards.text: Go to bed with a full cookie box, wake up to crumbs. Then terrors overtake him like a flood, and a tempest sweeps him away in the night.
Then the east wind carries him away, and he is gone, swept out of his place.

cards.question: As the wicked man flees headlong from the east wind, how does Job say it hurls itself against him?
Job pictures the east wind clapping its hands at the wicked man to welcome him back home.

cards.text: It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place. And that's where we'll leave Job for now, friend, but this story is far from over.
